source.title: Stacey: Promoting Stochastic Steepest Descent via Accelerated ℓp-Smooth Nonconvex Optimization
source.authors: Xin-Yu Luo; Cedar Site Bai; Bo-Lian Li; P. Drineas; Ruqi Zhang; Brian Bullins

record.tranche_reason: The study compares optimizers using training negative log-likelihood and test accuracy, but does not measure training classification error or test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR table reports training NLL for ResNet-18 trained from scratch, alongside test accuracy. Training NLL does not establish whether training classification error is zero or near zero. The paper also reports ImageNet and language-model results, which do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study develops and benchmarks an optimizer. Its CIFAR results report training NLL and test accuracy, without reporting training classification error or identifying CIFAR-10 versus CIFAR-100. It provides no comparisons of width-dependent spurious minima, depth degradation, initialization, learning-rate stability thresholds, or batch normalization that test V2–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' empirical conclusion: STACEY's primal-dual interpolation and task-dependent norm choices improve convergence and predictive performance over popular optimizers. They also establish a stationary-point convergence guarantee for stochastic ℓp descent under their assumptions. Their claim of consistent empirical superiority is stronger than the tables: STACEY does not beat every baseline at every checkpoint or on every metric.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces and evaluates S TACEY, an accelerated ℓp optimizer, and compares it with SGD with momentum, Adam, AdamW, and Lion; it does not reproduce the claim's experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: For CIFAR classification, the authors report the best performance with p = 2; for LLM pretraining, they report the best performance with p = 3.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 compares ResNet-18 training NLL across optimizers. Adam reaches 0.0083 at 200 epochs; STACEY variants reach 0.0021 and 0.0014. Lion's NLL rises from 0.1006 at epoch 50 to 0.2226 at epoch 100, then falls to 0.0245.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects reported CIFAR ResNet-18 training NLL; all listed optimizers have lower NLL at epoch 200 than epoch 50, but the reported trajectory is not uniformly decreasing.

record.problems: The CIFAR dataset is not specified as CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 in the supplied text. The reported training metric is NLL rather than classification error, so it cannot determine whether training classification error is near zero.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for test accuracy, ImageNet, or LLM pretraining: these do not measure the training classification-error behavior in the versions.

untested.parts: Training classification error on identified CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 datasets; corrupted labels; model-size, early-stopping, and regularization comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, spurious-local-minimum frequencies, and student overparameterization.
Depth-dependent training degradation and comparisons involving plain networks, residual shortcuts, special tanh initializations, or Fixup.
Initialization-dependent training speed, signal propagation, and trainable depth.
Loss recovery relative to initial stability thresholds, curvature drops, edge-of-stability dynamics, and threshold-related divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The record's claim that NLL decreases across every reported interval needs correction because Lion worsens at epoch 100. Low standard mean NLL can bound classification error, but these tables do not report that error directly or fully specify its evaluation conditions. Citations to Cohen et al. and use of ResNets do not themselves test V5 or V3.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, including effects of model size, random or corrupted labels, early stopping, and regularization.
Teacher-student two-layer ReLU problems, spurious minima, and width changes.
Depth effects, plain versus residual networks, and normalization.
Initialization comparisons, signal or gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss rises and recovery, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.
